claim: In a cohort of 18-36 year-old and 65-75 year-old individuals vaccinated with the 2014-2015 trivalent seasonal influenza vaccine, there was a five-fold reduction in the production of vaccine-specific antibodies in the serum of older persons compared to younger participants.
source: In our cohort of 18–36 year-old and 65–75 year-old individuals vaccinated with the 2014–2015 trivalent seasonal influenza vaccine (Figure 1A), there was a five-fold reduction in the production of vaccine-specific antibodies in the serum of older persons compared to younger participants (Figure 1B), consistent with previous reports (Govaert et al., 1994; Goodwin et al., 2006; Sasaki et al., 2011; Nakaya et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B and referenced to previous published studies.

claim: The diminished antibody production with age was associated with reduced formation of cTfh cells that are transcriptionally and clonally related to bona fide GC Tfh cells found in secondary lymphoid organs.
source: This diminished antibody production with age was associated with reduced formation of cTfh cells that are transcriptionally and clonally related to bona fide GC Tfh cells found in secondary lymphoid organs (Heit et al., 2017; Brenna et al., 2020; Hill et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies establishing the relationship between cTfh cells and GC Tfh cells.

claim: Prior to vaccination, the frequency of CXCR5+PD-1+++ CD4+CD45RA- cTfh cells was similar in the two age groups.
source: Prior to vaccination, the frequency of CXCR5+PD-1+++ CD4+CD45RA- cTfh cells was similar in the two age groups (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Seven days after vaccination there were significantly fewer circulating Tfh-like cells in older persons compared to the younger individuals.
source: Seven days after vaccination there were significantly fewer circulating Tfh-like cells in older persons compared to the younger individuals (Figure 1C,E), representing an impaired induction after vaccination when normalised to an individual's day 0 baseline (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C, 1E, and 1F.

claim: The GC-Tfh cell response to vaccination is impaired in older persons.
source: Together, these data indicate that the GC-Tfh cell response to vaccination is impaired in older persons.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing reduced cTfh cells in older persons after vaccination.

claim: After vaccination there is an increase in the number of Ki67+Bcl6+B220+ GC B cells in the draining inguinal LN in both younger 2-3 month-old adult and aged 22-24 month-old mice.
source: After vaccination there is an increase in the number of Ki67+Bcl6+B220+ GC B cells in the draining inguinal LN in both younger 2–3 month-old adult and aged 22–24 month-old mice (Figure 2A–C, gating strategy in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: The number of GC B cells was ten-fold lower in the aged mice ten days after immunisation, compared to younger adult mice.
source: However, the number of GC B cells was ten-fold lower in the aged mice ten days after immunisation, compared to younger adult mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The reduction in GC B cells in aged mice corresponded to a reduction in GC size.
source: This corresponded to a reduction in GC size (Figure 2D) and reduced levels of antigen-specific antibodies in the serum of aged mice (Figure 2E–G), consistent with previous reports that GC and antibody responses are reduced in magnitude in aged mice (Kosco et al., 1989; Szakal et al., 1990; Yang et al., 1996; van Dijk-Härd et al., 1997; Eaton et al., 2004; Linterman, 2014).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data in Figure 2D and cited previous studies.

claim: Aged mice have reduced levels of antigen-specific antibodies in the serum compared to younger adult mice.
source: This corresponded to a reduction in GC size (Figure 2D) and reduced levels of antigen-specific antibodies in the serum of aged mice (Figure 2E–G), consistent with previous reports that GC and antibody responses are reduced in magnitude in aged mice (Kosco et al., 1989; Szakal et al., 1990; Yang et al., 1996; van Dijk-Härd et al., 1997; Eaton et al., 2004; Linterman, 2014).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2E-G and cited previous studies.

claim: The deficiency in the GC response in aged mice was coupled with reduced numbers of total CXCR5hiPD-1hiFoxp3-CD4+ Tfh cells prior to, and ten days after immunisation.
source: This deficiency in the GC response was coupled with reduced numbers of total CXCR5hiPD-1hiFoxp3-CD4+ Tfh cells prior to, and ten days after immunisation, as well as significantly fewer antigen-specific Tfh cells, as assessed using 1W1K-loaded MHC-II tetramers (Figure 2H–M; gating strategy in Figure 2—figure supplement 1; key resources are listed in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2H-M.

claim: Aged mice have significantly fewer antigen-specific Tfh cells, as assessed using 1W1K-loaded MHC-II tetramers.
source: This deficiency in the GC response was coupled with reduced numbers of total CXCR5hiPD-1hiFoxp3-CD4+ Tfh cells prior to, and ten days after immunisation, as well as significantly fewer antigen-specific Tfh cells, as assessed using 1W1K-loaded MHC-II tetramers (Figure 2H–M; gating strategy in Figure 2—figure supplement 1; key resources are listed in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data using MHC-II tetramers shown in Figure 2H-M.

claim: Aged mice have impaired Tfh cell formation after immunisation, which recapitulates the age-associated defect in Tfh cell formation observed in humans.
source: This demonstrates that aged mice have impaired Tfh cell formation after immunisation, which recapitulates the age-associated defect in Tfh cell formation observed in humans (Figure 1).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of mouse data (Figure 2) with human data (Figure 1).

claim: After adoptive transfer of TCR-transgenic TCR7 or OTII CD4 T cells from 2 to 3 month-old mice into young adult hosts, more than 80% of all transgenic CD4+ T cells had undergone one or more cell divisions after immunisation.
source: After adoptive transfer of either TCR-transgenic TCR7 or OTII CD4 T cells from 2 to 3 month-old mice into young adult hosts, more than 80% of all transgenic CD4+ T cells had undergone one or more cell divisions after immunisation (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: Supported by CellTrace proliferation data shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: When cells from the same pool of TCR-transgenic T cells were transferred into 22-24 month-old recipient mice, significantly fewer T cells had completed more than one cell division.
source: In contrast, when cells from the same pool of TCR-transgenic T cells were transferred into 22–24 month-old recipient mice, significantly fewer T cells had completed more than one cell division (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: Supported by CellTrace proliferation data shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: Tfh cell differentiation of OTII CD4+ T cells isolated from 2 to 3 month-old mice was reduced three-fold ten days after immunisation in aged mice compared to younger recipients.
source: In addition to defects in T cell priming, Tfh cell differentiation of OTII CD4+ T cells isolated from 2 to 3 month-old mice was reduced three-fold ten days after immunisation in aged mice compared to younger recipients (Figure 3E–F), which was associated with reduced levels of antigen-specific antibodies in the serum of these mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E-F and ELISA data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: The aged microenvironment causes impaired early T cell activation and reduced Tfh cell development.
source: These observations indicate that the aged microenvironment causes impaired early T cell activation and reduced Tfh cell development.
evidence: Inferred from adoptive transfer experiments showing that young T cells have impaired responses in aged recipients.

claim: The reduced number of Tfh cells induced by immunisation in aged mice may be caused by defective T cell priming.
source: These data prompt the hypothesis that the reduced number of Tfh cells induced by immunisation in aged mice may be caused by defective T cell priming.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed defects in T cell priming in aged mice.

claim: After subcutaneous immunisation with Eα-GFP the majority of GFP+ antigen-bearing cells in the draining LN were CD11b+ cDC2s.
source: Consistent with these reports, after subcutaneous immunisation with Eα-GFP the majority of GFP+ antigen-bearing cells in the draining LN were CD11b+ cDC2s (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E; gating strategy from Guilliams et al. (2016).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-E and cited gating strategy.

claim: CD11b+ cDC2s likely belong to the migratory cDC2s subset, as pertussis toxin treatment, which disrupts G-protein coupled receptor-dependent cell migration, resulted in a reduced number of these antigen-presenting cells in the draining LN.
source: These cells likely belong to the migratory cDC2s subset, as pertussis toxin treatment, which disrupts G-protein coupled receptor-dependent cell migration, resulted in a reduced number of these antigen-presenting cells in the draining LN (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by pertussis toxin treatment experiment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and knowledge of pertussis toxin function.

claim: One day after immunisation, aged mice had half the number of total and GFP+ CD11b+ cDC2s compared to younger controls.
source: One day after immunisation, aged mice had half the number of total and GFP+ CD11b+ cDC2s compared to younger controls (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: The reduced number of cDC2s in aged mice was coupled with the reduced presentation of Eα peptide-MHC-II, despite normal total MHC-II expression on the cell surface.
source: This was coupled with the reduced presentation of Eα peptide-MHC-II, despite normal total MHC-II expression on the cell surface (Figure 3I–J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3I-J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The expression of the costimulatory ligands CD86, CD80 and the receptor CD40 on the surface of GFP+ CD11b+ cDC2s was diminished in aged mice, indicating impaired activation of cDC2s with age.
source: The expression of the costimulatory ligands CD86, CD80 and the receptor CD40 on the surface of GFP+ CD11b+ cDC2s was also diminished, indicating impaired activation of cDC2s with age (Figure 3K–P).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3K-P.

claim: Defective T cell priming in draining LNs of aged mice may be due to impaired antigen presentation and/or co-stimulation from the cDC2 subset.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that defective T cell priming in draining LNs of aged mice may be due to impaired antigen presentation and/or co-stimulation from the cDC2 subset.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the observed defects in cDC2 antigen presentation and co-stimulation.

claim: cDC2s from H2+/- mice present less peptide:MHC-II on their surface 22 hr after immunisation.
source: cDC2s from H2+/- mice present less peptide:MHC-II on their surface 22 hr after immunisation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H), but do not have an impaired capacity to prime CD4+ T cells three days after immunisation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I–J).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H-J.

claim: A reduction in antigen-presentation alone does not phenocopy the defect in T cell priming seen in aged mice.
source: This indicates that a reduction in antigen-presentation alone does not phenocopy the defect in T cell priming seen in aged mice, suggesting other age-dependent changes drive impaired T cell activation.
evidence: Inferred from the H2+/- mouse experiment showing normal T cell priming despite reduced antigen presentation.

claim: CD80/CD86 co-stimulation is critical for both T cell priming and Tfh cell differentiation.
source: CD80/CD86 co-stimulation is critical for both T cell priming and Tfh cell differentiation (Platt et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2015b).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Partially blocking CD80/CD86 co-stimulatory ligands using a CTLA4-Ig fusion protein in vivo results in a dose-dependent decrease in early T cell proliferation.
source: By partially blocking these co-stimulatory ligands using a CTLA4-Ig fusion protein in vivo, we observed a dose-dependent decrease in early T cell proliferation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K–L).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1K-L.

claim: Reducing the magnitude of CD28 signalling in vivo impairs Tfh cell differentiation.
source: Moreover, Wang et al. had previously demonstrated that reducing the magnitude of CD28 signalling in vivo impairs Tfh cell differentiation (Wang et al., 2015a).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study by Wang et al.

claim: The age-associated reduction in the expression of CD80/CD86 on cDC2s is a likely factor that contributes to impaired T cell priming and Tfh cell formation in aged mice.
source: This implicates the age-associated reduction in the expression of CD80/CD86 on cDC2s as a likely factor that contributes to impaired T cell priming and Tfh cell formation in aged mice.
evidence: Inferred from the CTLA4-Ig blocking experiments and previous studies on CD28 signalling.

claim: Principal component analysis demonstrated distinct clustering of cDC2 samples from young and aged mice with 47% of the variation in this dataset explained by age.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) demonstrated distinct clustering of samples with 47% of the variation in this dataset explained by age (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis identified one pathway that was underrepresented in cDC2s from aged mice: the cellular response to IFN-I.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis identified one pathway that was underrepresented in cDC2s from aged mice: the cellular response to IFN-I (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The underrepresentation of the IFN-I response pathway in aged cDC2s was driven by the reduced expression of the majority of IFN-I inducible genes in aged mice compared to younger adults.
source: This was driven by the reduced expression of the majority of IFN-I inducible genes in aged mice compared to younger adults (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Expression of Ifit1 and Mx1, canonical IFN-I stimulated genes (ISGs), were reduced in aged mice.
source: A reduction in the IFN-I response in cDC2s was confirmed by quantitative Real-Time PCR (RT-qPCR) in an independent cohort: expression of Ifit1 and Mx1, canonical IFN-I stimulated genes (ISGs), were reduced in aged mice (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: In unimmunised mice, the expression of Ifnb1 mRNA in the inguinal LN was not detectable.
source: In unimmunised mice, the expression of Ifnb1 mRNA in the inguinal LN was not detectable.
evidence: This is a direct observation from RT-qPCR experiments.

claim: Six hours after immunisation with Eα-GFP Ifnb1 is expressed in draining LNs, but the induction of Ifnb1 expression was three-fold lower in 22-24 month-old aged mice compared to 2-3 month-old adult mice.
source: Six hours after immunisation with Eα-GFP Ifnb1 is expressed in draining LNs, but the induction of Ifnb1 expression was three-fold lower in 22–24 month-old aged mice compared to 2–3 month-old adult mice (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: STAT1 phosphorylation levels and the upregulation of the ISGs Ifit1 and Mx1 in cDC2s were intact in aged mice upon ex vivo treatment with low levels of IFNα.
source: STAT1 phosphorylation levels and the upregulation of the ISGs Ifit1 and Mx1 in cDC2s were intact in aged mice upon ex vivo treatment with low levels of IFNα (Figure 4G–J).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4G-J.

claim: Aged cDC2s are capable of responding to IFN-I and do not exhibit cell-intrinsic defects in IFN signalling.
source: This indicates that aged cDC2s are capable of responding to IFN-I and do not exhibit cell-intrinsic defects in IFN signalling.
evidence: Inferred from the ex vivo IFNα treatment experiments showing intact responses in aged cDC2s.

claim: cDC2s derived from bone marrow stem cells from an aged, 23-month-old mouse transferred into an adult recipient mouse, do not exhibit age-associated defects in number and activation after immunisation when they develop and reside in the microenvironment of the younger host.
source: Consistent with this, cDC2s derived from bone marrow (BM) stem cells from an aged, 23-month-old mouse transferred into an adult recipient mouse, do not exhibit age-associated defects in number and activation after immunisation when they develop and reside in the microenvironment of the younger host (Figure 4K–M).
evidence: Supported by bone marrow chimera experiments shown in Figure 4K-M.

claim: The poor activation of cDC2s in aged animals is not linked with cell-intrinsic defects in their IFN-I response, but rather with impaired early induction of IFN-I in their microenvironment.
source: Together, these data suggest that the poor activation of cDC2s in aged animals is not linked with cell-intrinsic defects in their IFN-I response, but rather with impaired early induction of IFN-I in their microenvironment.
evidence: Inferred from ex vivo IFNα treatment and bone marrow chimera experiments.

claim: Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) and CD64+F4/80+ macrophages express the highest levels of Ifnb1 16 hr after immunisation.
source: This revealed that plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) and CD64+F4/80+ macrophages express the highest levels of Ifnb1 16 hr after immunisation (Figure 4N).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from sorted cell populations shown in Figure 4N.

claim: There is a potential link between age-associated defects in cDC2s and the reduced production of Ifnb1 by pDCs and macrophages.
source: This indicates a potential link between age-associated defects in cDC2s and the reduced production of Ifnb1 by pDCs and macrophages.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that pDCs and macrophages are the main Ifnb1 producers after immunisation.

claim: Age-associated defects in cDC2 activation coincided with reduced numbers of pDCs in aged, 22-24 month-old mice compared to adult controls upon immunisation.
source: In line with this, we found that age-associated defects in cDC2 activation coincided with reduced numbers of pDCs in aged, 22–24 month-old mice compared to adult controls upon immunisation (Figure 4O).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4O.

claim: The reduced number of pDCs in ageing is not an intrinsic feature of aged stem cells, but is driven by age-associated changes in their microenvironment.
source: To understand whether the reduction in pDCs was due to the aged microenvironment, we irradiated aged mice and reconstituted these mice with BM cells from 2 to 3 month-old animals. This revealed that the reduced number of pDCs in ageing is not an intrinsic feature of aged stem cells, but is driven by age-associated changes in their microenvironment (Figure 4P).
evidence: Supported by bone marrow chimera experiments shown in Figure 4P.

claim: In bone marrow chimeras, GFP+ CD11b+cDC2 cell numbers and the expression of CD80/86 on GFP+ CD11b+ cDC2 cells derived from young stem cells were reduced in aged BM recipients.
source: In these chimeras GFP+ CD11b+cDC2 cell numbers and the expression of CD80/86 on GFP+ CD11b+ cDC2 cells derived from young stem cells were reduced in aged BM recipients (Figure 4Q–S).
evidence: Supported by bone marrow chimera experiments shown in Figure 4Q-S.

claim: The poor activation of cDC2s in the LNs of aged animals could be driven by reduced numbers of IFN-I-producing pDCs due to age-related changes in their microenvironment.
source: Together, this suggests that the poor activation of cDC2s in the LNs of aged animals could be driven by reduced numbers of IFN-I-producing pDCs due to age-related changes in their microenvironment.
evidence: Inferred from bone marrow chimera experiments showing microenvironment-dependent reduction in pDCs and cDC2 activation.

claim: The expression of IFN-I inducible genes is increased in the blood of people in the first few days following vaccination.
source: As observed in mice, the expression of IFN-I inducible genes is increased in the blood of people in the first few days following vaccination (Nakaya et al., 2011; Athale et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: An early IFN-I gene signature peaks in the blood one day after vaccination in humans.
source: Using data from Henn and colleagues (Henn et al., 2013), an early IFN-I gene signature was identified after seasonal influenza vaccination in humans. This response peaks in the blood one day after vaccination (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by analysis of publicly available data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: IFN-I responsive genes were induced in older persons after influenza vaccination, but to a lesser extent than in younger people.
source: Application of this curated IFN-I vaccination signature to another dataset (Franco et al., 2013; Nakaya et al., 2015) showed that these genes were induced in older persons after influenza vaccination, but to a lesser extent than in younger people (Figure 5B), similar to our findings in aged mice (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by analysis of publicly available data shown in Figure 5B and comparison to mouse data.

claim: Day one samples from young people clustered distinctly from their pre-vaccination samples, whereas older persons showed a diminished early IFN-I response, as shown by a shorter IFN distance between day 0 and day 1 samples on the PCA plot.
source: Day one samples from young people clustered distinctly from their pre-vaccination samples, whereas older persons showed a diminished early IFN-I response, as shown by a shorter IFN distance between day 0 and day 1 samples on the PCA plot.
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis described in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The IFN-I distance was reduced by half in older compared to younger individuals (p<0.001).
source: The IFN-I distance was reduced by half in older compared to younger individuals (p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of PCA data.

claim: Increased IFN distances correlated positively with an increased neutralising antibody titre 28 days after vaccination.
source: Increased IFN distances correlated positively with an increased neutralising antibody titre 28 days after vaccination (Figure 5D–F), demonstrating a correlation between the early IFN-I response and antibody titres upon vaccination in people.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: There is a correlation between the early IFN-I response and antibody titres upon vaccination in people.
source: Increased IFN distances correlated positively with an increased neutralising antibody titre 28 days after vaccination (Figure 5D–F), demonstrating a correlation between the early IFN-I response and antibody titres upon vaccination in people.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: Blockade of IFN-I signalling prior to immunisation significantly reduced the expression of the co-stimulatory ligands CD80 and CD86 on cDC2s.
source: Blockade of IFN-I signalling prior to immunisation significantly reduced the expression of the co-stimulatory ligands CD80 and CD86 on cDC2s (Figure 6A–B), showing that a reduction of IFN-I signalling can partly recapitulate the ageing cDC2 phenotype.
evidence: Supported by anti-IFNAR1 blocking antibody experiments shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: A reduction of IFN-I signalling can partly recapitulate the ageing cDC2 phenotype.
source: Blockade of IFN-I signalling prior to immunisation significantly reduced the expression of the co-stimulatory ligands CD80 and CD86 on cDC2s (Figure 6A–B), showing that a reduction of IFN-I signalling can partly recapitulate the ageing cDC2 phenotype.
evidence: Inferred from the anti-IFNAR1 blocking experiments showing reduced CD80/CD86 expression.

claim: Absence of IFNαR in recipient mice results in reduced T cell proliferation of adoptively transferred IFNαR-sufficient ovalbumin-specific OTII cells three days after immunisation.
source: Furthermore, absence of IFNαR in recipient mice results in reduced T cell proliferation of adoptively transferred IFNαR-sufficient ovalbumin-specific OTII cells three days after immunisation (Figure 6C–D), similar to what had been observed in aged mice (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: Supported by adoptive transfer experiments in Ifnar1-/- mice shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: In the absence of IFNAR1 on DCs, there was a defect in Tfh cell formation seven days after immunisation.
source: To formally test the link between IFNαR signalling in DCs and Tfh cell formation, Ifnar1fl/fI:Itgaxcre/+ mice, that lack IFNαR on CD11c+ cells such as DCs, and their IFNαR-sufficient Ifnar1fl/fl:Itgax+/+ littermates were immunised with NP-1W1K in Alum. In the absence of IFNAR1 on DCs, there was a defect in Tfh cell formation seven days after immunisation (Figure 6E–H), without affecting serum levels of antigen-specific antibody at this early time-point (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by experiments in Ifnar1fl/fl:Itgaxcre/+ mice shown in Figure 6E-H.

claim: The lack of IFN-I signalling in DCs can mimic the age-associated impairment of Tfh cell differentiation.
source: This indicates that the lack of IFN-I signalling in DCs can mimic the age-associated impairment of Tfh cell differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the Ifnar1fl/fl:Itgaxcre/+ mouse experiments showing reduced Tfh cells.

claim: Imiquimod treatment increased expression of the ISGs Ifit1 and Mx1 in antigen-bearing cDC2s from both 2-3- and 22-24 month-old mice compared to age-matched no-imiquimod controls one day after immunisation.
source: Imiquimod treatment increased expression of the ISGs Ifit1 and Mx1 in antigen-bearing cDC2s from both 2–3- and 22–24 month-old mice compared to age-matched no-imiquimod controls one day after immunisation (Figure 7B–C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7B-C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Imiquimod treatment was associated with a two- to three-fold increase in the number of total and GFP+ CD11b+ cDC2s in draining LNs.
source: This was associated with a two- to three-fold increase in the number of total and GFP+ CD11b+ cDC2s in draining LNs (Figure 7D–E; Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–D) and with a two-fold increase in CD80 and CD86 on their surfaces (Figure 7F–G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7D-G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: Imiquimod treatment resulted in a two-fold increase in CD80 and CD86 on the surfaces of cDC2s.
source: This was associated with a two- to three-fold increase in the number of total and GFP+ CD11b+ cDC2s in draining LNs (Figure 7D–E; Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–D) and with a two-fold increase in CD80 and CD86 on their surfaces (Figure 7F–G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7F-G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: The enhancing effects of imiquimod on cDC2 numbers and activation were largely, but not completely, dependent on IFN-I signalling.
source: Topical imiquimod treatment of Ifnar1-/- and Ifnar1+/+ mice revealed that the enhancing effects of imiquimod on cDC2 numbers and activation were largely, but not completely, dependent on IFN-I signalling (Figure 7H–J).
evidence: Supported by experiments in Ifnar1-/- mice shown in Figure 7H-J.

claim: Imiquimod treatment can boost the reduced IFN-I response, and revert the numerical and co-stimulatory defects observed in cDC2s from aged mice.
source: This demonstrates that imiquimod treatment can boost the reduced IFN-I response, and revert the numerical and co-stimulatory defects observed in cDC2s from aged mice.
evidence: Inferred from the imiquimod treatment experiments showing increased ISG expression and cDC2 numbers/activation.

claim: Topical imiquimod treatment potently enhanced total and 1W1K-specific Tfh cell numbers in both 2-3- and 22-24 month-old mice seven days after immunisation.
source: Topical imiquimod treatment potently enhanced total and 1W1K-specific Tfh cell numbers in both 2–3- and 22–24 month-old mice seven days after immunisation (Figure 8A–F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8A-F.

claim: The boost in Tfh cell numbers by imiquimod was not dependent on intact IFN-I signalling in CD11c+ cells.
source: This boost in Tfh cell numbers was not dependent on intact IFN-I signalling in CD11c+ cells, as topical imiquimod treatment enhanced total and 1W1K-specific Tfh cell numbers in Ifnar1fl/fl:Itgaxcre/+mice to the same extent as in Ifnar1fl/fl:Itgax+/+ control mice seven days after immunisation (Figure 8G–H).
evidence: Supported by experiments in Ifnar1fl/fl:Itgaxcre/+ mice shown in Figure 8G-H.

claim: Imiquimod can enhance Tfh cells independently of IFN-I signalling in DCs, indicating TLR7 stimulation has multi-faceted roles in enhancing Tfh responses.
source: That imiquimod can enhance Tfh cells independently of IFN-I signalling in DCs indicates TLR7 stimulation has multi-faceted roles in enhancing Tfh responses.
evidence: Inferred from the Ifnar1fl/fl:Itgaxcre/+ mouse experiments showing imiquimod can boost Tfh cells without IFN-I signalling in DCs.

claim: Imiquimod treatment can restore cDC2 activation and Tfh cell differentiation in aged mice.
source: Together, these results show that imiquimod treatment can restore cDC2 activation and Tfh cell differentiation in aged mice.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of imiquimod treatment experiments.

claim: Imiquimod treatment was linked with a doubling of GC B cell numbers in aged mice, but not in younger animals.
source: This was linked with a doubling of GC B cell numbers in aged mice, but not in younger animals (Figure 8I–K).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8I-K.

claim: Imiquimod treatment did not affect serum levels of antigen-specific antibodies at the early time-point when most antibodies come from the extrafollicular plasmablast response.
source: Imiquimod treatment did not affect serum levels of antigen-specific antibodies at this early time-point when most antibodies come from the extrafollicular plasmablast response (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–C; MacLennan et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-C and citation to MacLennan et al.

claim: The humoral immune response to vaccination is diminished in older individuals, at least in part due to defects in the GC response.
source: The humoral immune response to vaccination is diminished in older individuals, at least in part due to defects in the GC response (Linterman, 2014; Gustafson et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The formation of Tfh cells is impaired in older persons and aged mice.
source: Here, we show that the formation of Tfh cells is impaired in older persons and aged mice.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: Topical application of the TLR7 agonist imiquimod corrected the age-dependent defects in cDC2s and increased the formation of Tfh and GC B cells in aged mice upon immunisation.
source: In mice, we show topical application of the TLR7 agonist imiquimod corrected the age-dependent defects in cDC2s and increased the formation of Tfh and GC B cells in aged mice upon immunisation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: The defect in the Tfh cell response in aged individuals is not irreversible, and can be corrected by exogenous stimuli.
source: This demonstrates that the defect in the Tfh cell response in aged individuals is not irreversible, and can be corrected by exogenous stimuli.
evidence: Inferred from the imiquimod treatment experiments showing restoration of Tfh cell responses in aged mice.

claim: A clinical trial has demonstrated that topical imiquimod treatment at the time of seasonal influenza vaccination enhances antibody responses to the vaccine in older persons.
source: Supporting our data, a clinical trial has demonstrated that topical imiquimod treatment at the time of seasonal influenza vaccination enhances antibody responses to the vaccine in older persons (Hung et al., 2014; Hung et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical trial studies.

claim: Changing vaccination approaches is a rational strategy for improving vaccine efficacy in older persons.
source: This, together with the data presented here, demonstrates that changing vaccination approaches is a rational strategy for improving vaccine efficacy in older persons, a challenge of increasing importance with the rising population age world-wide.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of the study and cited clinical trials.

claim: Ageing has been reported to impair DC activation.
source: Ageing has been reported to impair DC activation (Agrawal et al., 2007; Moretto et al., 2008), the production of IFN-I cytokines by pDCs in both humans and mice (Stout-Delgado et al., 2008; Panda et al., 2010; Sridharan et al., 2011; Agrawal, 2013; Agrawal et al., 2017), and the formation of Tfh cells (Garcia and Miller, 2001; Eaton et al., 2004; Lefebvre et al., 2012; Linterman, 2014; Gustafson et al., 2018; Nikolich-Žugich, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ageing has been reported to impair the production of IFN-I cytokines by pDCs in both humans and mice.
source: Ageing has been reported to impair DC activation (Agrawal et al., 2007; Moretto et al., 2008), the production of IFN-I cytokines by pDCs in both humans and mice (Stout-Delgado et al., 2008; Panda et al., 2010; Sridharan et al., 2011; Agrawal, 2013; Agrawal et al., 2017), and the formation of Tfh cells (Garcia and Miller, 2001; Eaton et al., 2004; Lefebvre et al., 2012; Linterman, 2014; Gustafson et al., 2018; Nikolich-Žugich, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ageing has been reported to impair the formation of Tfh cells.
source: Ageing has been reported to impair DC activation (Agrawal et al., 2007; Moretto et al., 2008), the production of IFN-I cytokines by pDCs in both humans and mice (Stout-Delgado et al., 2008; Panda et al., 2010; Sridharan et al., 2011; Agrawal, 2013; Agrawal et al., 2017), and the formation of Tfh cells (Garcia and Miller, 2001; Eaton et al., 2004; Lefebvre et al., 2012; Linterman, 2014; Gustafson et al., 2018; Nikolich-Žugich, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Brahmakshatriya and colleagues have demonstrated that transferring activated, in vitro BM-derived DCs into aged mice can boost both the GC and Tfh cell response upon immunisation.
source: In addition, Brahmakshatriya and colleagues have demonstrated that transferring activated, in vitro BM-derived DCs into aged mice can boost both the GC and Tfh cell response upon immunisation (Brahmakshatriya et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Age-associated defects in the early induction of IFN-I expression, probably by pDCs and macrophages, results in impaired expression of co-stimulatory molecules on cDC2s.
source: Our study demonstrates that age-associated defects in the early induction of IFN-I expression, probably by pDCs and macrophages, results in impaired expression of co-stimulatory molecules on cDC2s.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: The impact of reduced IFN-I stimulation on cDC2s in aged mice can be multifactorial: in DCs, IFN-Is promote the expression of co-stimulatory molecules and the cytokines IL-6, IL-27 and IL-1β.
source: The impact of reduced IFN-I stimulation on cDC2s in aged mice can be multifactorial: in DCs, IFN-Is promote the expression of co-stimulatory molecules and the cytokines IL-6, IL-27 and IL-1β (Luft, 1998; Moretto et al., 2008; Cucak et al., 2009; Batten et al., 2010; Gringhuis et al., 2014; Hassanzadeh-Kiabi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IL-6, IL-27 and IL-1β have been shown to enhance the expression of Bcl6, CXCR5 and ICOS by CD4+ T cells, thereby supporting differentiation towards the Tfh cell phenotype.
source: These molecules have been shown to enhance the expression of Bcl6, CXCR5 and ICOS by CD4+ T cells, thereby supporting differentiation towards the Tfh cell phenotype (Cucak et al., 2009; Barbet et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IL-6 production is reduced in DCs from aged mice.
source: In particular, IL-6 production is reduced in DCs from aged mice (Brahmakshatriya et al., 2017), which may act together with reduced co-stimulation to contribute to poor Tfh cell priming in aged mice.
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Reduced IL-6 production and reduced co-stimulation may act together to contribute to poor Tfh cell priming in aged mice.
source: In particular, IL-6 production is reduced in DCs from aged mice (Brahmakshatriya et al., 2017), which may act together with reduced co-stimulation to contribute to poor Tfh cell priming in aged mice.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the cited study and the findings of the current study.

claim: Treatment with the TLR7 agonist imiquimod at the time of immunisation restored IFN-I signalling in cDC2s in aged mice, increased their numbers in the draining lymph node and enhanced CD80/CD86 expression on their surface.
source: Treatment with the TLR7 agonist imiquimod at the time of immunisation restored IFN-I signalling in cDC2s in aged mice, increased their numbers in the draining lymph node and enhanced CD80/CD86 expression on their surface.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: IFN-I is an important signalling pathway to target to improve cDC2 functions in ageing.
source: This demonstrated that IFN-I is an important signalling pathway to target to improve cDC2 functions in ageing.
evidence: Inferred from the imiquimod treatment experiments showing restoration of cDC2 functions.

claim: IFN-I signalling in cDC2s was not uniquely required for the imiquimod-mediated increase in Tfh cell numbers in young mice.
source: However, IFN-I signalling in cDC2s was not uniquely required for the imiquimod-mediated increase in Tfh cell numbers in young mice.
evidence: Supported by experiments in Ifnar1fl/fl:Itgaxcre/+ mice showing imiquimod can boost Tfh cells without IFN-I signalling in DCs.

claim: Other, non-IFN driven effects of imiquimod, such as IL-6 production, can support Tfh cell formation.
source: This suggests that other, non-IFN driven effects of imiquimod, such as IL-6 production, can support Tfh cell formation (Schön and Schön, 2007; Walter et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The induction of IFN-I signalling in cells other than DCs, such as B cells or Tfh cells themselves may be sufficient to promote Tfh cells.
source: Alternatively, it may be that the induction of IFN-I signalling in cells other than DCs, such as B cells or Tfh cells themselves is sufficient to promote Tfh cells (Le Bon et al., 2006; Hervas-Stubbs, 2011; Nakayamada et al., 2014; Riteau et al., 2016; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The TLR7 agonist imiquimod can boost cDC2 and Tfh cells using more than one mechanism.
source: Together, this indicates that the TLR7 agonist imiquimod can boost cDC2 and Tfh cells using more than one mechanism, reinforcing its potential as a vaccine adjuvant.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results showing IFN-I-dependent and independent effects of imiquimod.

claim: Imiquimod treatment rescued the age-dependent defects in cDC2s and Tfh cell differentiation but did not fully restore GC B cell numbers or early antigen-specific antibody responses in aged mice to levels observed in younger adult mice.
source: In our experiments, imiquimod treatment rescued the age-dependent defects in cDC2s and Tfh cell differentiation but did not fully restore GC B cell numbers or early antigen-specific antibody responses in aged mice to levels observed in younger adult mice.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: The incomplete restoration of GC B cell numbers by imiquimod could be due to additional age-associated changes in other cell types involved in the GC and extrafollicular antibody response.
source: This could be due to additional age-associated changes in other cell types involved in the GC and extrafollicular antibody response (Linterman, 2014; Gustafson et al., 2018; Nikolich-Žugich, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Adoptive transfers of aged B cells into young hosts show that B cells from aged mice are capable of forming GCs in a young environment, suggesting that a B cell-intrinsic defect is not the cause of the poor GC response in aged mice.
source: However, adoptive transfers of aged B cells into young hosts show that B cells from aged mice are capable of forming GCs in a young environment, suggesting that a B cell-intrinsic defect is not the cause of the poor GC response in aged mice (Yang et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: B cell-extrinsic factors are implicated as additional contributors to the poor GC response in ageing.
source: These data therefore implicate B cell-extrinsic factors as additional contributors to the poor GC response in ageing.
evidence: Inferred from the cited study showing aged B cells can form GCs in young hosts.

claim: Both T follicular regulatory (Tfr) cells and FDCs have been linked to the age-dependent diminution of the GC response.
source: It is noteworthy that both T follicular regulatory (Tfr) cells and FDCs have been linked to the age-dependent diminution of the GC response.
evidence: This is a statement based on knowledge from the literature.

claim: Tfr cells are reported to be increased in number in aged mice and this overrepresentation of Tfr cells may result in excessive suppression of the GC response in older animals.
source: The GC response is negatively regulated by Tfr cells (Stebegg et al., 2018), that are reported to be increased in number in aged mice and this overrepresentation of Tfr cells may result in excessive suppression of the GC response in older animals (Sage et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is evidence that FDCs, stromal cells which are essential for the maintenance of the GC, are impaired in ageing.
source: There is also evidence that FDCs, stromal cells which are essential for the maintenance of the GC, are impaired in ageing (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: FDCs in aged mice form smaller networks and present fewer antigen-containing immune complexes on their surfaces after immunisation.
source: FDCs in aged mice form smaller networks and present fewer antigen-containing immune complexes on their surfaces after immunisation (Aydar et al., 2003; Turner and Mabbott, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Impaired FDC function is likely to affect the ability of B cells to capture antigen for presentation to Tfh cells, which in turn provide B cell growth and differentiation cues.
source: This is likely to affect the ability of B cells to capture antigen for presentation to Tfh cells, which in turn provide B cell growth and differentiation cues.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of FDC and Tfh cell functions.

claim: The age-associated defect in GC B cell expansion in mice is linked not only with a defect in T cell priming but also with other factors such as reduced antigen retention on FDCs and increased suppression by Tfr cells.
source: This suggests that the age-associated defect in GC B cell expansion in mice is linked not only with a defect in T cell priming but also with other factors such as reduced antigen retention on FDCs and increased suppression by Tfr cells.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the combined evidence from the study and cited literature.

claim: Several strategies are currently being used to enhance the response to vaccination in older persons, including modifications of adjuvants or administration of increased antigen doses.
source: Several strategies are currently being used to enhance the response to vaccination in older persons, including modifications of adjuvants (Frech et al., 2005) or administration of increased antigen doses (Remarque et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hung and co-workers have shown that topical imiquimod treatment at the time of vaccination enhances the antibody responses to influenza vaccination in both younger and older persons.
source: Hung and co-workers have shown that topical imiquimod treatment at the time of vaccination enhances the antibody responses to influenza vaccination in both younger and older persons (Hung et al., 2014; Hung et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The poor gut GC response in aged mice can be boosted by replenishing the gut microbiome with that of a younger animal.
source: We have previously shown that the poor gut GC response in aged mice can be boosted by replenishing the gut microbiome with that of a younger animal (Stebegg et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Age-related defects in the GC response are not irreversible and can be targeted therapeutically to improve immune responses in older individuals.
source: Together with the data presented here, this demonstrates that age‐related defects in the GC response are not irreversible and can be targeted therapeutically to improve immune responses in older individuals.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of the current study and cited previous work.

claim: Imiquimod can correct defective IFN-I signalling and the associated cellular defects in cDC2s, and can also boost Tfh cell formation in aged animals.
source: Because imiquimod can correct defective IFN-I signalling and the associated cellular defects in cDC2s, and can also boost Tfh cell formation in aged animals, this compound could play a key role in improving T-dependent vaccine responses, especially in the older members of our communities.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: Imiquimod could play a key role in improving T-dependent vaccine responses, especially in the older members of our communities.
source: Because imiquimod can correct defective IFN-I signalling and the associated cellular defects in cDC2s, and can also boost Tfh cell formation in aged animals, this compound could play a key role in improving T-dependent vaccine responses, especially in the older members of our communities.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study.
